opus-5.5.text:
I think they reflect it only partially, and the gap matters quite a lot for how we interpret progress.

Most benchmarks are built around tasks that are well-specified, self-contained, and automatically checkable. A math benchmark gives you a problem with a single numerical answer. A coding benchmark gives you a function to write or a GitHub issue to resolve, with unit tests that tell you whether you got it right. That's a very sensible design choice, because you need something you can grade at scale. But it means you're selecting for a particular slice of the work.

If you look at what a practicing mathematician actually does, a lot of it isn't solving a problem someone handed them. It's figuring out which questions are worth asking, noticing that two areas might be connected, developing new definitions and frameworks, reading the literature and realizing what's missing, and working on something for months where the answer isn't known in advance and there's no grader. Even FrontierMath, which we built at Epoch to be very hard, research-level problems that take experts hours or days, is still a set of problems with verifiable answers. That's a meaningful test of mathematical reasoning, but it isn't the same as producing a research program.

Software engineering is similar. Real engineering involves working in huge, messy codebases, coordinating with other people, understanding vague requirements from stakeholders, making architectural tradeoffs that only pay off or fail years later, debugging systems in production, and so on. Benchmarks like SWE-bench were a real step toward realism because they use actual repositories and actual issues, but they still tend to be fairly local changes with clear success criteria. The long-horizon, ambiguous, context-heavy parts of the job are underrepresented.

That said, I don't want to dismiss benchmarks. They do capture real, economically relevant skills, and the fact that models went from basically zero to strong performance on many of them in a few years is genuine evidence of capability gains. And the skills do transfer somewhat; being able to solve hard, well-posed problems is a prerequisite for a lot of the less structured work.

The way I'd put it is that benchmarks are a lower-dimensional projection of the job. They tell you a lot about the dimensions they measure, and much less about the others. So when a model saturates a benchmark, the right conclusion is usually not "this model can now do the job of a mathematician or engineer," but rather "this particular component is largely solved, and the bottleneck has moved to things like long-horizon agency, judgment, taste, and operating with poor feedback." Those remaining pieces may turn out to be harder, or they may fall faster than people expect, but our current benchmarks aren't great at telling us which. That's part of why I think we need more evaluations that look at extended, realistic tasks, and ideally measurements of actual usage and productivity in the real world, not just test scores.

r001.rationale: It contrasts well-specified benchmark problems with mathematical research that involves choosing questions, connecting areas, and developing a research program.

r002.rationale: It notes research can take months and describes long-horizon engineering work, contrasting these with benchmark tasks that are often completed locally.

r003.rationale: It says real engineering involves working in huge, messy codebases and that benchmarks underrepresent context-heavy work, even when using actual repositories.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they reflect it only partially, and the gap is important to be honest about.

Take something like FrontierMath, which we built at Epoch. The problems are genuinely hard, written by research mathematicians, and they resist the kind of memorization you worry about with older benchmarks. But what they test is a narrow slice of what a mathematician actually does. A real problem is well-posed with a verifiable answer. A practicing mathematician spends most of their time deciding what question is worth asking, figuring out whether a conjecture is even true, building the right abstractions, and writing proofs that persuade other people. Almost none of that shows up when you grade a numerical answer automatically. So a model can be very strong on the benchmark and still not be doing the thing that gets papers published.

Software engineering is similar. SWE-bench is a real improvement over toy coding problems, because the tasks come from actual repositories and you have to navigate existing code. But the tasks are scoped so that a pull request with a passing test suite counts as success. In practice engineers are working across long horizons: understanding what a user actually wants, negotiating requirements, maintaining systems for years, debugging things that aren't reproducible, coordinating with other people. The benchmark captures the thirty-minute-to-few-hour task, not the multi-week project.

That said, I'd push back on the idea that this makes benchmarks useless. They're measuring real capabilities, and the trend on them has been very fast. What I'd say is that they are leading indicators rather than direct measures of economic value. When models went from near zero to substantial performance on FrontierMath, that told us something true about reasoning ability, even if it didn't tell us mathematicians were about to be replaced. The right response is to keep extending the horizon of what we test, toward longer and messier tasks, and to look at adoption and productivity data alongside benchmark scores rather than reading either one in isolation.

r001.rationale: It says math benchmarks test a narrow slice of mathematical work, while research involves choosing questions, evaluating conjectures, developing abstractions, and writing persuasive proofs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts benchmark coding tasks lasting thirty minutes to a few hours with real engineering projects spanning multiple weeks.

r003.rationale: It says SWE-bench tasks come from actual repositories and require navigating existing code, rather than identifying missing codebase context as a difference.

astra-6.text:
I think they capture some important skills, but they’re quite far from capturing the whole job. These benchmarks tend to give you a well-defined problem, where it’s relatively easy to check whether you got the right answer. And that’s useful for measuring progress, but it leaves out a lot of what makes the work difficult in practice.

In mathematics, for example, a lot of the work is figuring out which questions are worth asking, developing useful definitions, and finding connections between different areas. Solving a problem someone has already formulated tests a narrower capability than doing mathematical research.

Similarly, in software engineering, writing a function from a clear specification is only part of the work. You also have to understand an existing codebase, figure out what someone actually wants, make design decisions, and maintain things over time. Often the specification itself is ambiguous or changes as you work.

So I’d take strong benchmark performance as evidence of capability on those particular tasks. I’d be more cautious about inferring that a system can do the full job. For that, you’d want evaluations involving longer projects, less clearly specified goals, and feedback from the people who actually use the results.

r001.rationale: It contrasts solving a problem already formulated with mathematical research, which includes deciding what questions are worth asking and developing useful definitions.

r002.rationale: It notes that real work involves maintaining software over time and recommends evaluations involving longer projects, identifying duration as a difference.

r003.rationale: It says software engineers must understand an existing codebase, a need omitted by benchmarks focused on functions with clear specifications.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they capture something real, but a fairly narrow slice of the work. Math benchmarks tend to give you a well-defined problem with a relatively short solution that you can check. Practicing mathematicians spend a lot of time deciding which questions are interesting, developing definitions, trying approaches that don't work, and building up ideas over much longer periods. Being good at solving competition problems is evidence of mathematical ability, but it isn't the same as being able to do mathematical research.

There's a similar issue with programming. A benchmark might ask you to write a function that passes some tests. A software engineer often has to figure out what should be built, understand a large existing codebase, negotiate ambiguous requirements, and maintain the result. Those things are harder to capture in a benchmark.

So I would take strong performance seriously, but be careful about the inference. It tells us that models can perform particular components of these jobs. How well that translates into doing the whole job depends on whether they can sustain that performance over longer tasks, handle ambiguity, and recover when something goes wrong.

r001.rationale: It contrasts well-defined benchmark problems with mathematical research, which involves choosing questions and developing ideas over time.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks often involve short solutions, while real work develops over longer periods and may require sustained performance on longer tasks.

r003.rationale: It says software engineers must understand a large existing codebase, a requirement not represented by the benchmark example of writing a function that passes tests.
